chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. Folding paper finds lines of symmetry, turning cut-outs finds angles of symmetry, and each idea is tested on rangoli, kolam, wheels and tiles from everyday life.

points.title: Fold it, turn it, then say it
points.text: Every new idea starts from a paper fold or a paper turn, so a line of symmetry and an angle of symmetry are first seen, then named.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the figure is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: Keeko's doubts

concepts.concept_name: Which pictures repeat a pattern?

content.text:
Look around you, you may find many objects that catch your attention. Some such things are shown below: [Flower, Butterfly, Rangoli, Pinwheel]
There is something beautiful about the pictures above.
The flower looks the same from many different angles. What about the butterfly? No doubt, the colours are very attractive. But what else about the butterfly appeals to you?
On the other hand, look at this picture of clouds. There is no such repetitive pattern.
We can say that the first four figures are symmetrical and the last one is not symmetrical. A symmetry refers to a part or parts of a figure that are repeated in some definite pattern.

concepts.concept_name: Mirror halves: the fold test

content.text:
Figure (a) shows the picture of a blue triangle with a dotted line. What if you fold the triangle along the dotted line? Yes, one half of the triangle covers the other half completely. These are called mirror halves!
What about Figure (b) with the four puzzle pieces and a dotted line passing through the middle? Are they mirror halves? No, when we fold along the line, the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

content.text:
Worked example: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?

2. Fold the puzzle pieces along their dotted line: the bumps and holes on the two sides do not match.
3. Only an exact match gives mirror halves.

content.text:
Worked example: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
1. Imagine a vertical line down the middle of each building.
2. Check that the left side matches the right side.
3. Clouds have no repeating pattern, so no symmetry.
Answer: Each of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram has a vertical line down the middle with the left half matching the right half, and many parts repeat in a pattern (towers, windows, tiers). The clouds have no repeating pattern, so they are not symmetrical.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1, first block): Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?
1. Try folding each picture along different lines.
2. Count the lines where the two halves match exactly: flower 6, rangoli 4, butterfly 1.
3. The pinwheel looks symmetric but its halves do not match when folded, and the cloud has no pattern.
Answer: Yes: the flower has 6 lines of symmetry, the rangoli has 4, and the butterfly has 1. The pinwheel and the cloud have no line of symmetry.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1, first block): For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle. 1) Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch 2) Kite 3) Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles 4) L-shape 5) Scalene triangle
1. Fold each shape in your mind and look for a line that makes both halves match.
2. The kite folds along its vertical diagonal; the L-shape folds along the diagonal through its corner.
3. The slanted quadrilateral and the scalene triangle have no matching fold.
Answer: Shape 1 has one line of symmetry (a slanted line through its tip). Shape 2 (kite) has one vertical line of symmetry. Shape 3 has none. Shape 4 (L-shape) has one diagonal line of symmetry through its corner. Shape 5 (scalene triangle) has none.

concepts.concept_name: Folding a square four ways

content.text:
Does a square have only one line of symmetry?
Take a square piece of paper. By folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
Here are the different folds giving different lines of symmetry.
Fold the paper into half vertically.
Fold it again into half horizontally (i.e., you have folded it twice). Now open out the folds.
Again fold the square into half (for a third time now), but this time along a diagonal, as shown in the figure. Again, open it.
Fold it into half (for the fourth time), but this time along the other diagonal, as shown in the figure. Open out the fold.
Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

content.text:
Worked example: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.
1. Fold each figure in your mind along vertical, horizontal and slanted lines.
2. Count the lines where both halves match.
3. The twisted petal flower never matches its mirror image, so no line.
Answer: Figure 1: 6 lines. Figure 2: no line of symmetry (it only has rotational symmetry). Figure 3: 4 lines (vertical, horizontal and the two diagonals).

3. Equal halves are not enough. The halves must overlap exactly, so a rectangle that is not a square has only 2 lines of symmetry, the vertical and the horizontal.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1, Punching Game block)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry? a) triangle with exactly one line of symmetry b) triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry c) triangle with no line of symmetry d) Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?
1. Two equal sides give one line: the line from the apex to the middle of the base.
2. All three sides equal give three lines.
3. If a triangle has two lines of symmetry it is forced to have all three, so exactly two cannot happen.
Answer: (a) An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). (b) An equilateral triangle. (c) A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.

1. Start with a symmetric shape such as a square or an arrow shape.

content.text:
So far we have been saying that when we fold a figure along a line of symmetry, the two parts overlap completely. We could also say that the part of the figure on one side of the line of symmetry is reflected by the line to the other side; similarly, the part of the figure on the other side of the line of symmetry is reflected to the first side! Let us understand this by labeling some points on the figure.
The figure shows a square with its corners labeled A, B, C and D. Let us first consider the vertical line of symmetry. When we reflect the square along this line, the points B, C on the right get reflected to the left side and occupy the positions occupied earlier by A, D. What happens to the points A, D? A occupies the position occupied by B and D that of C!

content.text:
Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1, Punching Game block): Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left. a) diagonals, red bottom segment b) diagonals, red left zigzag c) vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline d) vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline e) vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag f) vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline
1. Reflect the given red part in one blue line.
2. Reflect the new figure (old plus new) in the other blue line.
3. Check that both blue lines now act as folds.
Answer: Reflect the red part in the first blue line, then reflect the whole result in the second blue line. Then the figure is symmetric about both. concepts.concept_name: Ink Blot Devils

content.text:
So far we have seen symmetrical figures and asymmetrical figures. How does one generate such symmetrical figures? Let us explore this.
Ink Blot Devils
You enjoyed doing this earlier in Class 5. Take a piece of paper. Fold it in half. Open the paper and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half.
Now press the halves together and then open the paper again.
What do you see?
Is the resulting figure symmetric?
If yes, where is the line of symmetry?
Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts?
Try making more such patterns.
